paragraphs.heading: What the budget tracks
paragraphs.text: Earth's energy budget sets the energy the planet gets from the Sun against the energy it loses to space. Minor sources such as Earth's internal heat are included, but they add very little. The budget also follows how energy moves around inside the climate system. It covers the energy budget at the top of the atmosphere and at the surface, changes in the global energy inventory, and internal flows within the climate system.

paragraphs.heading: Uneven heating makes climate
paragraphs.text: The Sun warms the tropics near the equator more than the poles, so the sunlight each region gets is uneven. As energy moves to even itself out across the planet, it drives interactions among water, ice, air, rock and living things. The outcome is Earth's climate. The budget depends on many things, including aerosols, greenhouse gases, surface albedo, clouds and land use.

paragraphs.heading: Balance and imbalance
paragraphs.text: When energy in and out are equal, Earth is in radiative equilibrium and the climate is fairly stable. If more arrives than leaves, the planet warms; if more leaves, it cools. Many kinds of measurement show a warming imbalance since at least 1970, driven mainly by human changes to the atmosphere, with heating at a rate never seen before. From 2005 to 2019 the gap, called Earth’s energy imbalance (EEI), came to about 460 TW on average, or 0.90±0.15 W/m² across the globe.

paragraphs.heading: Slow to respond
paragraphs.text: Shifts in the budget take time to show up as real changes in global surface temperature. The delay comes from the thermal inertia of the oceans, the land and the cryosphere. Most climate models calculate this inertia accurately, along with energy flows and how much is stored.

paragraphs.heading: Sunlight in, longwave out
paragraphs.text: Averaged over the globe and the year, sunlight arrives at the top of the atmosphere at about 340 W/m², one quarter of the solar constant. Energy leaves as outgoing longwave radiation (OLR), and in the end all of it goes out that way. Sunlight itself holds a good deal of shortwave infrared, and a 4-micron wavelength is sometimes used to separate shortwave from longwave. Because Earth gives off about as much energy as it takes in, its temperature stays fairly constant.

paragraphs.heading: Small extras
paragraphs.text: Heat flowing out of Earth's interior is estimated at 47 terawatts (TW), split roughly evenly between radiogenic heat and heat remaining from the planet's formation. That works out to about 0.087 W/m² on average, just 0.027% of the energy budget at the surface. It is dwarfed by the 173000 TW of incoming solar radiation. All human energy production is smaller still, averaging 18 TW, or about 160,000 TW-hr across 2019.
